      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/sep/18/europe-ai-safety-debate</link>
      <description><p>Though Europe has measures that address how consumers might encounter AI, technology will impact them if the worst scenarios bear</p><p>Europe’s dilemma over AI was rendered in stark terms this week. The head of the continent’s central bank, Christine Lagarde, said Europeans have two options: shun the technology and lose out on growth; or embrace it and become dependent on tools developed by the US and China.</p><p>The great debate over AI safety that has erupted in recent days threatens to make the choice moot. If the worst scenarios come to bear – <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/sep/15/could-ai-really-wipe-out-humanity-and-hijack-the-internet">and experts have differing views on this</a> – then the technology will impact the continent regardless.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/sep/18/europe-ai-safety-debate">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <title>Your AI doomsday questions answered: ‘Why aren’t these companies being held to account?’</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/community/live/2026/sep/18/could-ai-really-end-humanity-technology-qanda</link>
      <description><p>After a week of alarming warnings about artificial intelligence’s potential to destroy the world as we know it, our technology reporters answered your questions on the reality of the AI threat </p><p></p><p><strong><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/community/live/2026/sep/18/could-ai-really-end-humanity-technology-qanda#comment-175632805">IcommentthereforeIam</a> asks:</strong> Given our senses, emotions, memory and moods, is it ever going to be accepted that humanly conscious AI is fantasy?</p><p><em><strong>Dan:</strong></em><strong> </strong>This is a serious question that has even rattled Richard Dawkins, the evolutionary biologist. He may not believe that God is real but he does believe that AI is conscious - or at least the chatbot he was using, which he called Claudia. “You may not know you are conscious, but you bloody well are,” he wrote.</p><p>And he’s not the first. In 2022 Google fired an engineer who went public with his belief that a company-developed AI had feelings. At the more troubling end of this belief, there are countless examples of people becoming overly attached to, and influenced by, AI chatbots – including cases of psychosis.</p><p><strong>Aisha: </strong>There’s certainly a theatrical – even <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/sep/10/anthropic-researchers-warn-ai-musk">“psy-op”</a>- quality to the flurry of AI doomsaying over the past weeks. It’s hard to say entirely what concrete developments are at the root of it all. We know that the <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/jul/22/openai-says-its-models-went-rogue-and-hacked-startup-in-unprecedented-incident">Hugging Face incident</a>, where a “swarm” of AI agents hacked another company, has been one trigger of the drama. There have been other contributing incidents too – Dario Amodei <a href="https://darioamodei.com/post/we-must-pace-the-frontier">suggests</a> internal developments at Anthropic have prompted his latest round of blogging, and there’s been some X discourse and doomy muttering about bioweapons.</p><p>We aren’t in the heads of Dario Amodei or Sam Altman, and so we cannot say how sincere they are, and how much they might have other goals in mind – such as, perhaps, <a href="https://www.reuters.com/legal/litigation/openai-ipo-will-not-happen-2026-amid-ai-safety-fears-altman-says-2026-09-12/">delaying their IPOs</a> until their finances look better. But any company of their size, and with their potential liabilities, would be angling hard to be regulated as favourably as possible. That’s what big companies do.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/community/live/2026/sep/18/could-ai-really-end-humanity-technology-qanda">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/politics/2026/sep/18/former-labour-deputy-leader-tom-watson-joins-palantir</link>
      <description><p>Peer takes full-time position at the controversial company as it fends off pressure from both Andy Burnham’s government and Sadiq Khan</p><p>Another former government minister has been hired by a controversial US AI company, this time Palantir, which has appointed Andy Burnham’s former ministerial colleague Tom Watson.</p><p>The Labour peer and former deputy leader will operate alongside Palantir’s UK and Europe chief executive, Louis Mosley, as the company attempts to fend off <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/politics/2026/jul/09/mps-urge-labour-to-ditch-330m-palantir-software-contract-with-nhs">pressure on Burnham’s government to axe its £330m NHS contract</a>.       <description><p>The first console I ever bought, it was hyped as a threat to the PlayStation, then mocked as a flop. But now, as it marks its 25th anniversary, it’s looked back on with misty-eyed reverence </p><p>This week marks the 25th anniversary of the Nintendo GameCube, the first console I ever bought with my own money. I vividly remember getting on the bus after school with a year’s worth of savings safely zipped into the pocket of my bag and going to a branch of Currys, where I dumped a bunch of notes, coins and vouchers on the counter to collect my pre-order. (It turned out that some of the vouchers from the previous Christmas had expired, but the guy at the checkout clearly felt so sorry for me that he redeemed them anyway. Released in Japan this week in 2001 (and in May 2002 in Europe), this surprisingly powerful purple cube sold much less than the Xbox and the PlayStation 2. With its squat, colourful form and unusual controller, arranged around a big traffic-light-green A button and small analogue sticks designed for small hands, it had a hint of Fisher-Price about it.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/games/2026/sep/16/small-but-mighty-remembering-nintendos-purple-cube-of-joy">Continue reading...</a></description>

Yet as the team grew, so did their ambitions. Created by Lionhead Studios for the original Xbox in 2004, it boasted cheeky charm alongside world-altering player choices, and its droll writing was brought to life in later iterations by national treasures such as Stephen Fry and Simon Pegg. Thanks to its unique blend of farce and fantasy, Fable grew into a globally beloved franchise – before Microsoft <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2016/mar/07/microsoft-closes-lionhead-studios-fable-legends">unceremoniously shuttered Lionhead in 2016</a>, after mandating that the studio turn its star series into a multiplayer game.       <description><p>We have a first play of the forthcoming Tomb Raider remake and speak with its developers. Can they improve on the gameplay without losing what made the 1996 original such a classic?</p><p>We join Lara Croft in St Francis’ Folly – inspired by the Unesco-listed monasteries of Meteora in Greece – as the light shines through the cracked ceiling and a flock of bats glide across the vast ruins below. When Lara leaps down to the monastery’s crumbling pillared courtyard, it becomes clear that these screeching, leathery creatures aren’t just set dressing. As they lurch towards her with unpredictable movements, she dispatches the swarm with a flurry of gun fire and panicked punches.</p><p>It’s a suitably cinematic reintroduction to our heroine and her very first adventure. Yet while our reunion gets off to an auspicious start, I have my concerns. It feels like reconnecting with an old friend at the pub, only for them to begin spouting conspiracy theories two pints in.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/games/2026/sep/11/tomb-raider-legacy-of-atlantis-lara-croft-remake">Continue reading...</a></description>

Insomniac’s three games based around the web-slinger are masterpieces of superhero wish fulfilment, allowing you to swoop above a depiction of Manhattan alive with graffiti artists, roving journalists and gun-toting gangsters. If anyone should be up to the task, it’s Wolverine. A beloved Marvel stalwart, his life much darker and bloodier than Peter Parker’s, he seems the ideal protagonist for a moody action adventure. Yet somehow this well-made game falls short of its potential.</p><p>Set years before the founding of the X-Men, Marvel’s Wolverine sees a disenfranchised Logan falling back in with Sabretooth and Mystique when their mentor Nathaniel Essex is kidnapped by mutant-hating billionaire Bolivar Trask. This archetypal tech bro has a disturbing plan for world domination and the X Team are out to stop him – but there is a secret buried in Wolverine’s past that’s about to cause an eruption. It’s a decent setup, filled with the sort of intrigue, violence and Freudian tension we expect from the X-Men.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/games/2026/sep/10/marvels-wolverine-review-a-gloriously-conflicted-lead-is-let-down-by-crude-boring-battling">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <description><p>Once hailed as the future, even the likes of Google, Sony and Microsoft have struggled to make streaming games fun, fast or affordable</p><p><strong>• </strong><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/info/ng-interactive/2021/nov/24/sign-up-for-pushing-buttons-keza-macdonalds-weekly-look-at-the-world-of-gaming"><strong>Don’t get Pushing Buttons delivered to your inbox? Sign up here</strong></a></p><p>In August 2009, at the very first Gamescom expo, I sat in a small meeting room in Germany and played Mario Kart and World of Warcraft on a laptop, via technology that was then completely new: cloud gaming. It was a demonstration for a yet-to-be-launched service called Gaikai that promised to let you play any game in a browser window, without a console. (Here is an <a href="https://www.ign.com/videos/real-time-demonstration">ancient video</a> of that demonstration, featuring a very young Keza.) With a single click I could launch into any game, hosted on servers hundreds of miles away. It really did look like the future.</p><p>Since then, plenty of companies have <a href="https://kotaku.com/top-gaming-people-say-streaming-that-frees-high-end-gam-1827695602">tried to be the first</a> to truly crack game streaming, vying to be the Netflix of games. Sony ended up buying Gaikai for $380m (£242m) in 2012; its technology now powers the streamable classic games library on PlayStation, and the PS5’s advanced game streaming. OnLive, Gaikai’s first competitor, launched in 2011 but shut down after less than a year, leaving Sony to acquire all its patents. Google’s Stadia cloud gaming service also imploded, launching in 2019 and shutting down three years later.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/games/2026/sep/09/streaming-from-the-cloud-was-meant-to-changes-games-forever-what-happened">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <title>Lenore review – incel’s obsession with online influencer turns into anatomy of dislocated digital-age mindset</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/sep/14/lenore-review-incels-obsession-with-online-influencer-turns-into-anatomy-of-dislocated-digital-age-mindset</link>
      <description><p>Digital-age Australian psychodrama tracks the shut-in mania of dangerously disaffected male fan, but doesn’t get inside his mind</p><p>If the <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/media/2022/feb/13/too-close-for-comfort-the-pitfalls-of-parasocial-relationships">parasocial phenomenon</a> is a kind of hell, then Max Wren, protagonist of this Australian digital-age psychodrama, resides in the ninth circle. Self-barricading in a basement room surrounded by screens, working on a documentary about the object of his disaffection (an enigmatic influencer called Lenore), this obsessive shut-in makes Eminem’s Stan look like the Dalai Lama. Touching on subjects including the attention economy, the male gaze, and incel isolation and misogyny, director David Ward feels both Max and Lenore’s pain. But his ungainly debut film doesn’t fully transcend its stage origins to capture the splintered headspace of the terminally online.</p><p>Like films about fictional pop stars that feature unconvincing music, it doesn’t help that the quickfire résumé of Lenore’s career only half-conveys her magnetism. A one-time beauty influencer called Veronica Brand, she later graduates to more extreme performance art-type stunts, such as livestreaming her miscarriage; a move that, spliced without her knowledge into a children’s TV broadcast, forced her into hiding. But this performative vulnerability, including hints of her abusive dad, apparently won her legions of OnlyFans-style acolytes. Not just Max, but also his colleague Sam (Sam Macdonald), a brash interloper outraged to find he was nothing special to Lenore and who turns up at Max’s door offering exclusive footage of her.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/sep/14/lenore-review-incels-obsession-with-online-influencer-turns-into-anatomy-of-dislocated-digital-age-mindset">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <description><p>Pilot project in Preston comes with apprenticeship offer for Neets at end of three-week course</p><p>In a <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign/2026/feb/19/a-safe-space-to-come-and-just-be-the-longed-for-radical-utopian-return-of-britains-youth-clubs">youth centre opposite Preston bus station</a>, the UK government is trying to address two of the greatest challenges facing the national economy: AI and youth unemployment.</p><p>The hope is that one will solve – rather than cause – the other.
